question: The Commission’s establishment of an EU certification framework for permanent carbon removals, carbon farming, and carbon storage in products marks a significant step towards integrating agricultural practices with climate goals. This is particularly relevant for Irish farmers, who are positioned to contribute to carbon sequestration efforts through enhanced land-management practices.

The initiative not only aims to incentivise sustainable farming practices but also opens potential new revenue streams through the generation and trading of certified carbon units. With Ireland’s rich agricultural heritage and our shared commitment to the Paris Agreement, the EU certification framework for carbon removals presents a unique opportunity for Irish farmers and combating climate change. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that this framework not only supports Irish farmers in transitioning to sustainable practices but also effectively integrates with existing environmental and agricultural policies?

Additionally, can the Commission clarify if it will introduce a carbon system similar to Australia’s Carbon Farming Initiative, which allows farmers to earn carbon credits by storing carbon or reducing greenhouse gas emissions on the land?
answer: The provisional agreement on the regulation in object (1) integrates environmental objectives and agricultural policy: i) it sets minimum requirements of do no significant harm principle for several environmental objective s (2); ii) it requires biomass to be compliant with EU sustainability criteria laid down in Directive (EU) 2018/2001 (3); iii) it introduces for carbon farming the obligation to generate co-benefits for biodiversity and eco-systems, including soil health as well avoidance of land degradation; iv) it introduces more links with the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), in the definition of operators, on the role of public support for enabling factors (4); v) it recognises the potential of the CAP’s identification system for agricultural parcels (LPIS) to reduce the cost of verification.

The regulation also extends the scope of the carbon farming certification to reduction of soil emissions, including emissions from fertilisers, and it requires the Commission to develop a pilot methodology for livestock emissions.

The regulation does not regulate the end-use of certified units, in order to avoid double regulation with other horizontal EU legislation dealing with climate-related reporting and claims, such as the directive on corporate sustainability reporting (5) and the proposed Directive on Green Claims (6).

A recent study commissioned by the Commission looked into policy options to mitigate climate change in agriculture by putting a price on emissions and rewarding carbon farming (7). During 2024 and 2025 the Commission will organise more technical workshops to discuss the impacts of this and other related policy approaches.
